title: Incremental Fact Fluency
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane describes building a set of multiplication-fact worksheets around "incremental rehearsal," a research-backed strategy for students who don't pick up times tables through ordinary practice: focus on one new fact family at a time while continually mixing in facts students already know. Working through fact families in a deliberate sequence (2s, 10s, 5s, 4s, 3s, 11s, 9s, 6s, 8s, 7s), each new worksheet devotes half its problems to the new family and half to review, with skip-counting and mini-whiteboard checks preceding each new handout. Kane used AI to generate the large volume of worksheets needed, describing a laborious back-and-forth prompting process, and explains his reasoning for not timing students, arguing that timed tests risk stoking math anxiety and measuring processing speed rather than mathematical knowledge.
points: Kane's core instructional principle -- break a skill into small pieces, focus on one at a time, keep practising the old pieces while introducing new ones -- is presented as generalisable well beyond multiplication facts.
His fact-family sequence (2s, 10s, 5s, 4s, 3s, 11s, 9s, 6s, 8s, 7s) is a deliberately reasoned ordering, starting with confidence-building facts and ending with the hardest-to-retain ones.

Kane frames math anxiety as arising specifically from practice that doesn't feel like it's working -- students who know they're not improving -- which is why the incremental, visibly-progressing structure matters as much as the content itself.

His candid account of using AI to generate the worksheets ("dozens of attempts," tweaking prompts repeatedly) is a useful counterweight to hype: AI saved him from undoable manual labour but was far from a one-shot solution.
quotes: If students don't seem to make progress with a skill, a good strategy is to take that skill, break it down into smaller pieces, focus on one piece at a time, and gradually build up to the larger skill.
It's called "incremental rehearsal." Incremental rehearsal is a strategy for students who are struggling to learn their math facts.
I think the biggest cause of math anxiety is being asked to do something over and over, yet feeling like you're not getting better at it.
I generated these using AI. I've checked them and I don't think there are any mistakes, but I could be wrong.
I literally needed dozens of attempts before the AI could get the handout right. I prompted multiple different LLMs over and over again.
For math facts, that means breaking the facts down into smaller groups and gradually expanding the pool of facts that students can retrieve from memory.
